t: What To Do If Attacked By A Student
q: According to the American Psychological Association, 44 percent of teachers report being physically attacked by a student.
If attacked by a student, there are two places you must be to stay safe. Only two. The first is beyond striking distance. Meaning, out of range of your attacker.
Within the one to six foot zone that is the attacker’s striking distance. It is here that you will suffer the greatest amount of injury and physical damage.
So what happens if a student closes on you and into your danger zone while throwing violent punches and/or kicks? So fast that you can’t get away? You close on them.
As soon as you make contact, wrap your arms around them, grip one hand around your opposite wrist (in a monkey grip), place your ear tight to their chest, and hang on tight.
Either they will be injured or you will. It will also encourage other students to jump in. You’ll lose your job and need a good lawyer.
x: The one-to-six-foot 'danger zone' around an attacker is where the greatest physical damage occurs and should be avoided or moved through quickly.
If attacked, the safest options are either escaping entirely beyond striking distance or, if escape is impossible, closing the distance to bear-hug the attacker.

Question sessions become “gotcha” sessions where the leader points out how they could have done the work better.
Micromanagers experience high turnover and burnout on the teams they lead.
Team members don’t feel trusted or responsible when working for micromanagers, and therefore under-deliver and underperform for them.
Even if it worked (which it doesn’t, by any standard), micromanaging leaders fail to recognize that this brand of leadership isn’t scalable.

Good leaders eschew micromanaging behavior, preferring to clarify roles and responsibilities and letting people drive toward results on their own.
By staying in their own lane, the best leaders develop a team that feels trusted and engaged.

t: How To Handle The Student Disrespect Sweeping The Country
q: Since returning to in-person learning, respect has taken a nosedive.
You must take up space by standing tall with your shoulders back and head up. Walk and move with purpose or stand still and in one place .
You must speak boldly. Use your adult voice, even with younger students. Be clear and unwavering.
When you speak, let your instructions and directives hang heavy in the air. Wait them out. Let them settle. Say your peace and then zip it.
When you show that it doesn’t get under your skin, that you don’t take their disrespect personally, students stop doing it.

t: Depressurizing Emotion: How to Calm a Hostile Written Conversation Using BIFF
q: We educators are especially bound to run into hostile communications from time to time. With so many students, parents, colleagues, and bosses in our daily sphere, even the best of us are bound to find ourselves in conflict from time to time.
So when a hostile message does come in, my aim is repair — after all, winning battles like these is almost always a net loss. I don't want to win.

Keep it Brief. The more words, the more chances we create for communication to fail and the hostility cycle to deepen. If the parent is angry about a grading practice, no need to enumerate your philosophy on grading.

As the old, great teacher John Wooden sometimes said, your character is what you actually are while your reputation is what you appear to be. Attend to your character — which you're doing by defusing a hostile conversation before it ignites — and your reputation will take care of itself in due time.

I think it's possible to read a hostile communication impersonally, respond to it well, and also take to heart where we might be able to improve in the future. I can't think of a single conflict in my life where I didn't contribute at least one percent to the conflict's genesis.
Now, in circumstances of abuse, gaslighting, etc. — forget my caveats completely. We'll perform poorly, even in the inner work of morally engaging with a hostile other, when under too much pressure.
x: Stuart addresses a near-universal hazard of working with people — parents, colleagues, bosses, students — over email: the hostile message that attacks your character.
He frames the underlying goal as repair rather than victory, arguing that 'winning' a hostile exchange is almost always a net loss for a working relationship you have to sustain.

t: Depressurizing the Body: The Bummer about Bedtime Revenge
q: But here's the problem (spoiler alert): bedtime revenge wins in the end. Because while we temporarily get that sweet moment of blissful sovereignty, it comes at the cost of waking up tomorrow with greater physical pressurization, which in turns diminishes our odds of experiencing autonomy in our normal waking hours.
It's us taking revenge on a day where we didn't experience much autonomy by stealing some free time from the stubbornly large number of hours that our bodies supposedly need to sleep.

Things started to change for me when I read a book about sleep and realized I was being a fool. So I started trying to get 7-8 hours per night, and it took me months before I started feeling the difference.

I used to dislike power naps because I felt so much pressure to fall asleep in the 15-20 minutes that I'd give myself for the nap. The pressure greatly reduced the restorative effects of the 15-20 minutes, and it often left me awake the whole time.
Dude. You don't have to fall asleep during a power nap. Just get comfortable and close your eyes for 15-20 minutes.
The most efficient nap is the nappucino. The caffeine won't fully engage in your bloodstream for about twenty-five minutes, so drink up right before you lie down.
Even as a kid, I often had to read a book in order to fall asleep. To make this less annoying to your spouse or partner, get them a sleep mask.
x: Bedtime revenge feels like reclaiming autonomy but actually reduces it, because the sleep debt it creates diminishes the next day's capacity for genuine autonomy.

t: A Simple Way To Get Better At Classroom Management
q: It’s to keep a record of every misbehavior. You see, the simple act of tracking is shown to improve performance no matter the field.

According to research, keeping a journal of everything you eat results in greater weight loss. (One 1,700 person clinical trial at Kaiser Permanente showed twice as much weight loss as those who didn’t keep a journal.)
Keeping score, so to speak, sparks an intense desire to improve—even if you do nothing else but notice your numbers, regardless of whether they went up or down.
Practically, what keeping a record does for classroom management is cause you to be more consistent.
It also helps shift your focus away from your students, and how their misbehavior annoys and frustrates you, and toward your ability to influence and change their behavior.
It shows you in a way you can’t deny that it’s not about your students. It’s about you and your own performance.
x: Keeping a brief written daily record of every misbehavior and its consequence is proposed as a simple habit that improves consistency over time.
The recommendation is grounded in self-monitoring research, including a cited Kaiser Permanente trial where food-journal keepers lost roughly twice as much weight as non-journalers.
Tracking works psychologically, similar to video-game scoring systems, by creating an internal motivation to improve simply through visible numbers.

Linsin proposes a low-effort daily habit for improving classroom management: keeping a written record of every misbehavior, the specific behavior, and the consequence given, reviewed briefly at the end of each day.
The practice reorients a teacher's focus away from frustration with students and toward their own performance and agency.
